Enhancement of surfactant biodegradation with an anaerobic
membrane bioreactor by introducing microaeration
Zhenmin Cheng a, b, Yuansong Wei a, b, *, Qingqing Zhang c, Junya Zhang a, b, Tiedong Lu d,
Yuanmei Pei e
a State Key Joint Laboratory of Environmental Simulation and Pollution Control, Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of
Sciences, Beijing, 100085, China

c Renmin University of China, Beijing, 100872, China
d Guangxi University, Nanning, 530004, Guangxi, China
e Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou, 730050, Gansu, China
h i g h l i g h t s
 Microaeration effectively enhanced biodegradation of anionic surfactants.
 The swift degradation followed the kinetic characteristics of zero order reaction.
 The biodegradation processes were clearly illustrated by 3D-EEM and SEC results.
 Speciﬁc genera of bacteria involving with biodegradation processes were found.

a b s t r a c t
In controlled ecological life support system (CELSS), 100% water recycle efﬁciency is needed. Both water
and nutrients in wastewater needs reclaiming. In an anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) designed
to hydrolyze organic matters and convert organic nitrogen, accumulation of anionic surfactants and
organic compounds was observed in the supernatant. To solve the problem, microaeration which had
rarely been reported to enhance surfactants biodegradation in anaerobic process was introduced and it
was proved to be an effective approach that resulted in concentrations of surfactants and soluble
chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) in the supernatant decreasing from 9000 mg/L and 40000 mg/L to
2000 mg/L and 10000 mg/L, respectively. And the degradations followed the kinetic characteristics of
zero order reaction with R2 values of 0.9472 and 0.949. Three-dimensional excitation emission matrix
(3D-EEM) analysis revealed that some activities of microbes were activated and enhanced by microa-
eration, which resulted in the disintegration of aggregates of large molecules, indicated by the size
exclusion chromatography (SEC). After the introduction of microaeration, the emerging genera Aqua-
microbium, Flaviﬂexus, Pseudomonas and Thiopseudomonas in the microbial community might be
responsible for the effective biodegradation of the surfactants.

1. Introduction
Controlled ecological life support system (CELSS) is an artiﬁcial
closed ecosystem built for long-term space exploration which
provides humans (astronauts) with enough breathable air, clean
water, essential food and safe working-living places (Dai et al.,
2018). In the CELSS, urine and greywater need properly treating
and a 100% water recovery rate is essential to ensure the material
closure of the whole system. And all the waste treatment systems
have to feature high performance, small foot prints, and as little
consumables and by-products (such as gas emission and excess
sludge) as possible. In 1990s, National Aeronautics and Space
Administration (NASA) made an estimation of 20e30 L/(d$person)
wastewater in the CELSS (Wieland, 1994; Wydeven and Golub,

1990). And results from the recent 4-person-180-day integrated
experiment inside a CELSS conducted in China which employed a
combined AnMBR-MBR system (our previous work) in wastewater
treatment and reuse process indicated that an average of 51 L
wastewater was produced per day (Li and Zuo, 2017). Compared
with a water consumption of 75e220 L/(d$person) for city's resi-
dential use (Ministry of Construction of the People's Republic of
China, 2002), the much lower water consumption in the CELSS
results in higher concentration of surfactants contained in personal
care products and detergents in the wastewater. In NASA's
advanced life support project, greywater recycling was studied
through the use of a ﬁxed-ﬁlm bioreactor, with higher than
600 mg/L surfactant (Igepon TC-42) in the inﬂuent (Levine et al.,
2000).
Anionic surfactants, as core components of detergent and
cosmetic products formulations, contribute signiﬁcantly to the
pollution proﬁle of sewage and wastewaters of all kinds. In the
CELSS, puriﬁed wastewater is usually recycled into the hydroponic
system. Surfactants have been considered to have phytotoxic ef-
fects (Bubenheim et al., 1997) and their accumulation in the hy-
droponic system may be barely avoided, so they have to be
eliminated as possible. Surfactants at high concentrations in
wastewater can be eliminated effectively by coagulation or foam
separation (Beltran-Heredia et al., 2012; Srinet et al., 2017). But
such processes produce large quantity of solid waste, making them
not suitable for the CELSS. Though surfactants are degradable or
readily degradable under aerobic condition (Lechuga et al., 2016),
they can give rise to some problems such as foaming and long
retention times in the wastewater treatment (McAvoy et al., 1993).
Thus treatment of undiluted wastewaters under anaerobic condi-
tions may partially surmount this difﬁculty (Shcherbakova et al.,
1999). However, surfactants have been shown to inhibit the
anaerobic bioprocess (Feitkenhauer and Meyer, 2002) and results of
some studies (J. Krueger et al., 1998; Scott and Jones, 2000) have
demonstrated the persistence of surfactants under anaerobic con-
ditions. Microaeration i.e. some amount of oxygen is introduced to
a basically anaerobic biochemical process (Botheju and Bakke,
2011) has been applied to enhance the anaerobic bioprocess.
Some studies showed that under proper experimental conditions,
mainly an appropriate amount of air or oxygen introduced, and
enhancement of hydrolysis (Wu et al., 2015), sulﬁde oxidation (van
der Zee et al., 2007), elevation of methane yield (Tartakovsky et al.,
2011), and degradation of refractory and toxic organic compounds
(Zitomer and Shrout, 1998) have been achieved. Whereas whether
or not effective biodegradation of surfactants can occur under
microaeration condition has remained unknown during anaerobic
treatment.
In this study, an AnMBR in the combined AnMBR-MBR system
for wastewater treatment and reuse was used to treat synthetic
CELSS wastewater. The AnMBR was controlled under hydrolysis-
acidogenic stage aiming at realizing ammoniﬁcation, primary
breakdown of complex organic compounds and in the meanwhile
avoiding large amount of biogas production according to re-
quirements of the CELSS. Compared to some high strength waste-
water such as that is produced by food manufacturing process,
CELSS wastewater has much less organic compounds, which means
its biochemical methane potential is correspondingly much lower.
And what's more, methanogenenic process needs longer hydraulic
retention time (HRT) that demands bigger footprint, and the sys-
tematic complexity of CELSS will be higher for utilizing methane.
So, maybe it’s better to employ a hydrolysis-acidogenic process as
the initial stage of the CELSS wastewater treatment. Therefore, the
purpose of this study was to investigate performance of the AnMBR
with the introduced microaeration, especially on anionic surfac-
tants
biodegradation,
including
characteristics
of
surfactants
degradation, transformation of dissolved organic matters (DOM)
and evolution of microbial community, in order to provide tech-
nical support for the CELSS wastewater treatment and reuse.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Description of the AnMBR
The AnMBR comprised an anaerobic bioreactor and two
pressure-driven external cross-ﬂow tubular membrane modules
(MO P1U(0.5 m)_I8, Beijing Tri-high Membrane Technology CO.,
Ltd, PVDF, 0.03 mm pore size, 0.011 m2 ﬁltering area) in series
(Fig. 1). The cross-ﬂow rate of the mixed liquor was kept above
2.5 m/s by a centrifugal pump (CRN 1s-2, Grundfos) to control
membrane fouling, and the permeate ﬂux was set at around 27 L/
(m2$h). The anaerobic bioreactor was a continuous stirred-tank
reactor. It was made of polymethyl methacrylate and had a diam-
eter of 190 mm and a height of 700 mm. And it was sealed with a
cover plate to prevent uncontrolled gas emission. A buffer tank also
made of polymethyl methacrylate with a maximal working volume
of 78 L was used to store the synthetic wastewater. An air
compressor was used to supply limited amount of air into the
anaerobic bioreactor. To avoid severe foaming problem, the air was
introduced through a plastic tube with an inner diameter of 3 mm.

Excess sludge was regularly discharged with a sludge pump ac-
cording to a speciﬁc sludge retention time (SRT). The system ran
automatically under control of a programmable logic controller
(PLC) (S7-200, Siemens).
2.2. Synthetic wastewater
Synthetic wastewater used in this study was made up of two
parts, i.e. synthetic urine and greywater. The recipe of synthetic
urine was according to Chutipongtanate and Thongboonkerd
(2010) and Verostko et al. (2004). Amounts of detergent constitu-
ents such as toothpaste, body lotion and liquid soap etc. in the
synthetic greywater were estimated based on a 4-person crew that
produced about 50 L wastewater altogether per day. And other
organic compounds were added according to Chu et al. (2005). The
surfactants in the synthetic wastewater were sodium lauryl sulfate
(SLS) and sodium lauryl polyoxyethylene ether sulfate (SLES) which
were two typical sorts of anionic surfactant used in detergents. The

2.3. Operation and sampling
The AnMBR was seeded with concentrated excess sludge from a
municipal wastewater plant with an anaerobic/anoxic/oxic (A2/O)
process at capacity of 550,000 m3/d in Beijing. Before this study, the
AnMBR had run for 5 months treating this synthetic wastewater.
During the ﬁrst 60 days of this study, the mixed liquor suspended
solids (MLSS) in the reactor was maintained at 29.8 ± 2.95 g/L and
decreased to 15.9 ± 2.85 g/L afterwards because some sludge was
purged out of the AnMBR for some other experiments. Sample of
sludge (100 mL) was taken once a week and 40 mL sludge was
discharged every day, resulting in a SRT of 243 d. The HRT was set at
20 h. As shown in Table 1, during the ﬁrst 68 days, no air was
introduced into the AnMBR and in the following periods different
amounts of limited air were introduced with a ﬁshbowl air
compressor with power capacity of 20 W. An ORP of 200 mV or
lower was maintained throughout the whole experimental period.
Although the AnMBR ran at ambient temperature, the temperature
of the mixed liquor was maintained between 33 and 38 C due to
the continuous circulation. Samples of inﬂuent and permeate were
taken at least twice a week. Supernatants were collected by
centrifuging mixed liquor at 10000 rpm for 10 min. Samples of
inﬂuent, supernatant and permeate were kept at 4 C and sam-
ples of mixed liquor were kept at 20 C before analysis.
2.4. Analytical methods
2.4.1. Water quality
Ammonia and total nitrogen (TN) in the inﬂuent and AnMBR
permeate were analyzed according to the Standard Methods
(APHA, 2005). Chemical oxygen demand (COD) was measured us-
ing HACH 8000 methods with a DR 2800 spectrometer (HACH,
USA). SCOD was measured with the ﬁltrate samples through
0.22 mm membrane (SCAA-1202, Anpel, China). Methylene blue
active substances (MBAS) assay was carried out to determine
anionic surfactants concentration using HACH Crystal Violet
Method (Method 8028) and the result was expressed as mg MBAS/
L. MLSS and mixed liquor volatile suspended solids (MLVSS) were
determined at 104 C (4 h) and 600 C (2 h), respectively.
2.4.2. Measurement of DOM
Concentrations of six volatile fatty acids (VFAs) namely acetic
acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, iso-butyric acid, valeric acid and
iso-valeric acid were analyzed by a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu
GC-2010 Plus, Japan) equipped with a ﬂame ionization detector and
stabilwax-DA column (0.32 mm  25 m  0.25 mm) as described
previously (Zhang et al., 2016). The total concentration of VFAs was
described as mg COD/L.
A Varian Eclipse ﬂuorescence spectrophotometer (F-7000,
Hitachi, Japan) was used to acquire 3D-EEM ﬂuorescence spectra of
the ﬁltered supernatants in different experimental stages. The
spectrometer used a xenon excitation source and displayed a
maximum emission intensity of 10000 arbitrary units (AU). EEM
spectra were gathered with scanning emission (Em) spectra from
220 to 550 nm at 5 nm increments by varying the excitation (Ex)
wavelength from 200 to 400 nm at 5 nm increments. The spectra
were recorded at a scan rate of 12000 nm/min, using excitation and
emission slit bandwidths of 5 nm (He et al., 2017). Three Ex/Em
regions (Region I: Ex 200e250 nm and Em 280e330 nm; Region II:
Ex 200e250 nm and Em 330e380 nm; Region III: Ex 250e380 nm
and Em 280e380 nm) of the EEM spectra were analyzed using the
ﬂuorescence regional integration (FRI) method (Chen et al., 2003).
The percent ﬂuorescence response (Pi,n) of samples in different
stages were calculated as follows (Chen et al., 2003):

sludge sample was centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 10 min, and the
pellet was used for DNA extraction using FASTDNA Spin Kit for Soil
(MP Biomedicals, USA) in triplicate according to manufacturer's
instructions, and the resulting extracts were composited to average

the extracted DNA were determined through 1% agarose gel elec-

PCR primers 515F/806R targeting the bacteria and archaea 16S
V4 region were selected for the microbial community structure
analysis. The reverse primer contains a 6-bp error-correcting bar-
code unique to each sample. The barcode was permuted for each
sample and permitted the identiﬁcation of individual samples
within a mixture in a single Illumina MiSeq sequencing run. DNA
was ampliﬁed in triplicate for each sample following a protocol
described previously (Zhang et al., 2016). PCR amplicons were
further puriﬁed using a DNA puriﬁcation kit (BioFlux, Japan), and
the concentrations were determined by spectrometry using a
QuantiFluor™-ST (Promega, USA). Amplicons from different sam-
ples were then mixed to achieve equal mass concentrations in the
ﬁnal mixture, which were sent out to Sangon Co., Ltd. in Shanghai
for small-fragment library construction and pair-end sequencing
using the Illumina MiSeq sequencing system (Illumina, USA).
Sequencing reads were assigned to each sample according to the
unique 6-bp barcode for each sample. Pairs of reads from the
original DNA fragments were merged using FLASH and then were
ﬁltered using QIIME quality ﬁlters. PCR chimeras were ﬁltered out
using UCHIME, and the rest sequences were normalized to fairly
compare the samples in the same sequencing depth. The taxonomic
classiﬁcation of the sequences in each sample was carried out
individually using RDP Classiﬁer, and the sequences of different
taxonomy levels were assigned at the bootstrap cutoff of 50%, as
suggested by the RDP. In addition, diversity and richness indices
were calculated using the relevant RDP pipeline modules.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of the AnMBR
Throughout the whole experimental period, the inﬂuent COD
concentration was steadily around 1300 mg/L, and it could be
divided into two sub-periods according to the COD removal efﬁ-
ciency. As shown in Fig. 2(a), in Stage I without microaeration the
efﬂuent COD concentration was 800e1000 mg/L, resulting in COD
removal efﬁciency between 25 and 40%. While in Stage II and III,
introduction of microaeration resulted in lower efﬂuent COD con-
centration of 400e800 mg/L and higher COD removal efﬁciency of
40e70%. It was worth noting that just after the introduction of
microaeration, the efﬂuent COD concentration rose sharply for a
few days (Day 76e82), with the highest value of 1750 mg/L. Fig. 2(b)
shows that during Stage I VFAs in the efﬂuent accounted for about
70% COD and during the Day 76e82 there was not obvious VFAs
concentration increasing. So this stream of high COD efﬂuent could
mainly contain some biodegradation products of complex organic
compounds that had not been degraded to VFAs yet. And this will
be further discussed in the next section. In other words, these days
played a role of delay period, after which the COD concentration
declined quickly to 500 mg/L and maintained steadily below
600 mg/L until the air ﬂux was reduced. With decreasing of COD in
efﬂuent, sharp reduction of VFAs was also observed. In petro-
chemical wastewater pretreatment using hydrolysis-acidiﬁcation
process, Wu et al. (2015) reported that proper limited aeration
with dissolved oxygen (DO) under 0.3 mg/L had a positive effect on
VFAs production compared to the control reactor, but the produc-
tion of VFAs decreased signiﬁcantly when DO was higher than
0.3 mg/L. Similar results were shown during improved anaerobic
co-digestion of brown water and food waste by microaeration (Lim
et al., 2014). VFAs are easily degradable carbon sources, so the high
aeration condition could have further oxidized the generated VFAs
(Botheju and Bakke, 2011). Thus the microaeration ﬂux was
reduced in Stage III and subsequently the VFAs to COD ratio of the
efﬂuent gradually rose back to 60e80%.
The performance of the AnMBR on nitrogen transformation is
shown in Fig. 2(c). In the inﬂuent organic nitrogen namely urea
took the dominant proportion of TN, and the ammonia nitrogen
concentration was only 70e80 mg/L. Under the activities of
ammonifying bacteria, almost all the urea was transformed into
ammonia nitrogen and the ammonia nitrogen concentration of the
efﬂuent took a percentage of above 90% of TN, whatever with or
without microaeration. This indicated that the oxygen introduced
by the microaeration was nearly completely consumed in the
hydrolysis-acidogenic process involved with organic carbon com-
pounds biodegradation. The performance of the AnMBR on nitro-
gen transformation and VFAs production proved that it was
running well at the hydrolysis-acidogenic state as designed.
3.2. Accumulation and degradation of surfactants in the AnMBR
Fig. 3(b) shows that the MBAS concentration of inﬂuent was
about 110 mg/L throughout the whole experimental period. In
Stage I the MBAS concentration of efﬂuent was 40e70 mg/L most of

trogen transformation (c).

346

the time. However it was soon discovered that the reduced sur-
factants were not actually degraded but retained in the AnMBR by
the separation of tubular membrane, which was reﬂected by the
high MBAS concentration of supernatant in the AnMBR even above
10000 mg/L. The molecular weight of SLS and SLES are not too big
to make themselves retained by the tubular membrane. When
dissolved in water at low concentration surfactant molecules exist
as monomers. The concentration of surfactant at which the ther-
modynamics of the surfactant-solvent system favor micelle for-
mation is called the critical micelle concentration (CMC). At
concentrations higher than the CMC surfactants have the ability to
solubilize signiﬁcantly more of a hydrophobic organic compound
than would dissolve in water alone (D. Haigh, 1996). That is to say,
at concentrations above the CMC, surfactants will connect with
more organic matter with their hydrophobic groups and thus
format complex compounds whose size are big enough to be
intercepted by the membrane separation. The SLS and SLES con-
centrations in Stage I were obviously higher than their CMC values
proposed by Tolls and Sijm (1995) and Tokiwa (1968), respectively.
And this resulted in the sustaining accumulation of the surfactants
and other organic compounds in the AnMBR contributing to the
SCOD concentration as high as 40000 mg/L in the supernatant as

shown in Fig. 3(a).
The accumulation of surfactants and other organic compounds
was apparently a serious problem that threatened the steady
operation of the AnMBR. As microaeration had been proven effec-
tive to enhance the hydrolysis-acidiﬁcation process (Wu et al.,
2015), it was introduced into the AnMBR in this study. The MBAS
concentration
of
the
supernatant
decreased
promptly
from
9000 mg/L to about 2000 mg/L when the descending speed began
to slow down. And the SCOD concentration of the supernatant
showed the same trend of evolution, which conﬁrmed the fact that
the high SCOD concentration had been caused by the accumulation
of surfactants. Fig. 3(c) and (d) shows that during the ﬁrst half of
Stage II, degradation of surfactants and SCOD followed the kinetic
characteristics of zero order reaction with R2 values of 0.9472 and
0.949. It was worth noting that during the Day 71e85, the MBAS
concentration of the efﬂuent was obviously increased at the highest
value of 199 mg/L. This was the reason why during these days the
efﬂuent COD concentration was increasing sharply (Fig. 2(a)). And
in Fig. 3(a) it could be seen that the descending speed of SCOD was
relatively slow during the ﬁrst few days in Stage II. In this period,
something might happen like this: the introduced oxygen caused
physical-chemical and biological changes in the mixed liquor, and
some surfactant molecules were cut from attached organic com-
pounds but large-scale degradation of these separate organic
compounds and surfactant molecules had not started yet. So large
quantities of surfactant molecules went through the membrane
and caused the rising of MBAS and COD concentrations of efﬂuent.
To further investigate the detailed variation caused by the
microaeration, 3D-EEM analysis was conducted. The three super-
natant samples were collected in different experimental stages. In
Fig. 4, three types of ﬂuorophores representing tyrosine-like pro-
tein (Region I), tryptophan-like protein (Region II) and soluble
microbial by-product-like material (Region III) (Chen et al., 2003)
were observed and data within the corresponding three regions
were analyzed. It could be seen that without microaeration only
ﬂuorophore appeared in Region I. And along with the extension of
microaeration, ﬂuorophore showed up in Region III and became
stronger. In the meantime the ﬂuorophore in Region I migrated
towards Region II. Further more, results of FRI analysis (Table 2)
revealed that from the day 43 to day 225 the percent ﬂuorescence
response PI,n decreased from 78.5% to 53% while on the other hand
PII,n and PIII,n increased from 14.9% to 29.7% and 6.6%e17.3%,
respectively. As the name suggests, soluble microbial by-product-
like material is usually produced by microbial activities. So the
signiﬁcant boost of PIII,n indicated that under microaeration life
vitality of microbes in the AnMBR was activated and enhanced af-
terwards, which was responsible for the subsequent reductions of
MBAS and SCOD. Amino acid composition is a sensitive indicator for
the degradation of organic matter and it has been reported that
during organic matter degradation acidic species tyrosine decrease
(Wu and Tanoue, 2001). Tryptophan-like ﬂuorescence is related to
microbial activity and may be created by microbial activity within
the system (autochthonous) (Gone et al., 2009). A linear relation-
ship between the BOD5 of wastewater and their corresponding
ﬂuorescence intensities at 340 nm exists using an excitation
wavelength of 280 nm (Reynolds and Ahmad, 1997). These ﬁndings
were consistent with the evolution of DOM substances indicated by
3D-EEM analysis in this study.
Recently SEC has been used to fractionate organic matter in the
environmental engineering processes (Guo et al., 2017). As different
molecules with the same molecular weight may have different
sizes, the standard substance used for SEC should have the same
molecular structure type as the testing samples to acquire accurate
results (Kr Egeberg and Alberts, 2003). The DOM in this study had
too complex constituents to be determined on the AMW using a
known standard substance. But from the SEC results we could still
get the AMW distribution information of DOM. In Fig. 5, peaks of
efﬂuent samples from different experimental stages appeared in a
broad range from 6 to 16min. The large molecules with peak
appearing in 6e8 min could be complex micelle-like matter con-
taining surfactants and organic compounds, while medium and
small molecules with peak appearing in 12e16 min could represent
intermediate metabolites and VFAs. Under microaeration the rela-
tive intensity of large molecules decreased and the representing
peak nearly disappeared at last whereas there was an obvious in-
crease in the number of small molecules (15e16 min). The variation

3.3. Microbial community evolution
The high coverage values of OTUs (97% similarity) (Table 3)
demonstrated that the sequencing depth was enough to reﬂect the
microorganisms' proﬁle in the inoculum and samples from
different experimental stages. The Shannon and Simpson indexes
showed that operational conditions exerted signiﬁcant inﬂuence on
the microbial community diversity. Under complete anaerobic
condition the microbial community diversity was greatly decreased
and microaeration had a positive effect on increasing it. But the
variation could also have been the result of the continuous
declining surfactants concentration.
In Stage I Firmicutes and Proteobacteria which were two of the
three dominant phyla in the inoculum were enhanced whereas
Bacteroidetes disappeared (Fig. 6 (a)). Firmicutes has been reported
to play critical roles at hydrolysis and acidiﬁcation stages (Zheng
et al., 2013). And this study indicated that this phylum could
resist high concentration of SLS and SLES.
Stage II was a period when the large amounts of accumulated
surfactants were biodegraded effectively. Under microaeration
condition in this period Proteobacteria was further enhanced but
the dominant class became Alphaproteobacteria instead of Gam-
maproteobacteria (Fig. 6 (b)) and the phylum Actinobacteria rose
accounting for a percentage of 29%. The emerging genus belonging
to Actinobacteria was Flaviﬂexus (Fig. 6 (c)) which was proposed by
Du et al. (2013) with the type species Flaviﬂexus huanghaiensis. The
facultatively anaerobic species was positive for the activity of
esterase lipase and could hydrolyze starch and gelatin. Among the
dominant class Alphaproteobacteria Aquamicrobium was the major
genus. All members of the genus Aquamicrobium have been isolated
from pollutant-loaded environments such as wastewater treatment
plants, activated sewage sludge and bioﬁlters (Jin et al., 2013). Some
species afﬁliated to Aquamicrobium have been reported to produce
varieties of enzymes such as esterase and esterase lipase and thus
they were able to degrade complex organic compounds such as
petroleum hydrocarbon (Wang et al., 2015) and a wide range of
aryloxyphenoxypropionate herbicides (Wang et al., 2017).

supernatant while the bacterial community further evolved. The
dominant genera became Thiopseudomonas and Pseudomonas, both

reported unable to grow under anaerobic condition (Jin et al., 2013),
which could have been the reason why the class Alphaproteobac-
teria signiﬁcantly decreased when the air ﬂux was reduced in this
period. The facultatively anaerobic genus Thiopseudomonas was
afﬁliated to the class Gammaproteobacteria. It was proposed in 2015
by Tan et al. (2015) with the type species Thiopseudomonas deni-
triﬁcans which was isolated from sludge of an anaerobic, deni-
trifying, sulﬁde-removal bioreactor. The genus Thiopseudomonas
was also positive for activities of esterase and esterase lipase, like
Aquamicrobium and Flaviﬂexus. The ability to produce these
involving enzymes may have been responsible for the degradation
of surfactants. Compared with Thiopseudomonas, Pseudomonas also
afﬁliated to the class Gammaproteobacteria is a quite older genus. It
was described in 1894 and is one of the most diverse and ubiqui-
tous bacterial genera whose species have been isolated worldwide
in all kinds of environments (Peix et al., 2009). Roig et al. (1998)
proved that immobilized Pseudomonas C12B was effective SLS
degrading biocatalyst and the experimental result proposed by
Jovcic et al. (2010) showed that Pseudomonas sp. ATCC19151
degraded all SLS present in the liquid medium (up to 4% w/v of SLS)
within 48 h at 30 C. And recently two strains isolated from a MBR
that efﬁciently degraded SLES were conﬁrmed to belong to the
genus Pseudomonas (Karray et al., 2016).
4. Conclusion
The anionic surfactants SLS and SLES in the inﬂuent accumu-
lated in the supernatant of the AnMBR during the hydrolysis-
acidogenic
process.
Introduced
microaeration
effectively
decreased the concentration of surfactants from 9000 mg/L to
2000 mg/L without foam emerging or signiﬁcant mineralization of
VFAs. DOM fractionation results revealed that microaeration
enhanced the activities of microbes and led to the disintegration of
aggregates of large molecules. Under microaeration condition
variation occurred in the bacterial community and the genera
Aquamicrobium, Flaviﬂexus, Pseudomonas and Thiopseudomonas
might be responsible for the biodegradation of the surfactants. All
these results show that microaeration is a valuable approach under
hydrolysis-acidogenic condition in CELSS wastewater treatment
and reclamation process.
